FamilySearch volumes are indexed under both 'San José de Ocoa, Peravia, Dominican Republic' and 'San José de Ocoa, San José de Ocoa, Dominican Republic' — search BOTH place names in any volume or catalog search.

Civil birth registration in San José de Ocoa started locally ca. 1858, well before Law 659 of June 1944 that formally standardized civil registration nationwide. Records are real and usable; do not assume pre-1944 records are absent.

Because a birth had to be registered within 30 days or face penalties, many children were registered late (Reconocimientos/late registrations). Two digitized Reconocimientos volumes (1908–1924 and 1924–1940, each ~94% indexed + full-text) capture births from earlier decades — always search these if the civil birth register for the target year is missing or yields no result.

Most civil marriage registers for San José de Ocoa from 1889–1913 are 0% name-indexed and NOT full-text searchable — they must be browsed image-by-image. The exception is vol. 005190819_008 (1893–1911 marriage records), which is full-text searchable despite having no name-index percentage.

Catholic baptismal records (Bautismos) run from at least 1862 and are largely 84–98% name-indexed + full-text searchable via FS collection 1918910. For persons born before or whose civil birth is missing, the baptismal record is the primary substitute and is often more legible and better indexed than early civil registers.

Civil birth volume 004591120 covers 1858–1870 and 1879–1903 and is 100% name-indexed but NOT full-text searchable — use name search via FamilySearch record_search, not fulltext_search, for this volume.

San José de Ocoa falls in the Diocese of Baní (under the Archdiocese of Santo Domingo). Earlier parish records may be held at the diocesan archive in Baní or at the local parish rather than at a civil registry.

All records are in Spanish. Older registers (pre-1900) use 19th-century Spanish handwriting; a reading aid such as the FamilySearch Spanish Handwriting Tutorial (https://script.byu.edu/spanish-handwriting/introduction) is recommended.

FamilySearch's Getting Started page states civil registration was not consistent until 1944, but this refers to the national law, not local practice. San José de Ocoa has extant civil registers from 1858 onward and should be searched for the full 1860–1940 window.

74 digitized volumes were identified for San José de Ocoa (1860–1940). The survey reviewed 50; 24 additional volumes exist and may include further birth, marriage, or death registers not listed here — check the FamilySearch Catalog entry for San José de Ocoa civil registry (catalog ID 2031186) for the complete set.

# Locality Guide: San José de Ocoa, Dominican Republic (1860–1940)

## Jurisdictional Context

San José de Ocoa was founded on **5 March 1845**. Until 2000 it was a municipality within **Peravia province** (capital: Baní); in 2000 it became the capital of its own province of the same name. For the research period 1860–1940, all records were created under the Peravia provincial structure. FamilySearch digitization indexed these volumes inconsistently under both `San José de Ocoa, Peravia, Dominican Republic` and `San José de Ocoa, San José de Ocoa, Dominican Republic` — **always search both** place names.

The municipality is in the **Diocese of Baní** (Archdiocese of Santo Domingo). It contains three modern municipalities: San José de Ocoa (cabecera), Rancho Arriba, and Sabana Larga.

## Civil Registration Records

**Background:** The Dominican Republic adopted civil registration influenced by the Napoleonic Code beginning as early as 1823 (Bayaguana). Local registers for San José de Ocoa survive from **1858**. The national Law 659 of June 1944 formalized the system but did not create it — usable civil records predate 1944 by decades.

### Civil Births (Nacimientos)

| Coverage | Image Group | Indexed | Full-text | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1858–1870, 1879–1903 | 004591120 | 100% | No | FS record search (name index) |
| 1884–1888 | 104873512 | 94% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1894–1896 | 004318923, 105113002 | 59–70% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1898–1907 | 004591121_001 | 93% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1904–1906 | 105113024 | 92% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1907–1910 | 105113010 | 99% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1910–1912 | 004591121_002/003, 104873513 | 91% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1912–1916 | 004591121_004 | 98% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1917–1922 | 004591121_005, 104869660, 004591122_001/002 | 92–99% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |
| 1922–1925 | 104870965 | 64% | Yes | FS record search + fulltext |

**Coverage gap:** 1870–1879 not found in the surveyed 50 volumes.

**Late registrations (Reconocimientos):** Two volumes capture births registered years late:
- 1908–1924 (vol. 104875611): 94% indexed + full-text searchable
- 1924–1940 (vol. 104875612): 94% indexed + full-text searchable

Always check Reconocimientos if the target birth year's register is missing or yields no result.

fields.resolution_rationale:
The given name of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas's mother is disputed: 'Fidelina' in two derivative FamilySearch indexes versus 'Petrona' in the original handwritten civil death register. The correct name is needed to record and research this woman (tree stub I2).

The derivative indexes src_001 (6H3-5D6R) and src_003 (6TMN-HQ51) both name 'Fidelina Chalas' as mother. These are modern transcriptions of the original register page produced by indexers reading the handwritten text remotely; neither indexer had personal knowledge of the family. src_006, the original Act No. 255 (7 Nov 1978, San José de Ocoa), names 'Petrona Chalas' as mother — this is the physical civil register entry signed by Dr. Luis Giordano Maceo before the civil registrar.

The original register (src_006, 'Petrona') is authoritative. In genealogical source hierarchy, an original contemporaneous official record supersedes a derivative transcription. Two derivative indexes agreeing on 'Fidelina' does not overcome this hierarchy because both index the same handwritten page and are not independent — they may share or compound the same misread.

The 'Fidelina' reading is a derivative transcription error. In Dominican cursive script of this era, the handwritten capital letters 'P' (for Petrona) and 'F' (for Fidelina) can look similar when the descending stroke of a 'P' does not close its loop clearly, producing a form resembling 'F' with a short cross-bar. Both 'Petrona' and 'Fidelina' are recognizable Spanish given names, making an unwitting substitution easy. The second index either independently repeated this misread or followed the first. This is a documented pattern of derivative transcription error: an indexer substituting a plausible given name for a misread one, where the original's handwriting settles the question conclusively.

exhaustive_declaration.justification: All seven stop criteria are met or confirmed unavailable after exhaustive search. The prior blocking criterion — two unsearched avenues (Reconocimientos volumes and Catholic baptism browse) — has been resolved: pli_009 searched both Reconocimientos volumes (104875611 and 104875612) directly by volume ID at 94%+ indexed coverage (zero hits), and pli_010 searched the target baptismal volume 005190819_004_M9SP-M12 by fulltext including the highly diagnostic '+Carmen +Nida' query (zero hits at 92% FT coverage). No civil birth, Reconocimiento, or baptism for Marina López exists in any accessible repository. Marina's own original civil death register (src_009, Act 256, 5 Oct 1984) names father Manolo Lopez (fallecido) and mother Carmen Nida Lopez (fallecida) — an original official civil registration act explicitly designed to record the deceased's parents. The parentage information is secondary (physician informant Dr. Luis Octavio Medina Melo was not present at Marina's birth), but the record is original and official, uncontradicted by any other source, and supported by negative FAN evidence eliminating two other Manuel López families in San José de Ocoa 1913. Independent verification could not be achieved because no corroborating surviving record exists — this is a 'no further known sources' exhaustion, not an unsearched gap. Research is reasonably exhaustive; proof-conclusion should set the honest evidentiary tier the single-source-unit finding supports.

No known repository for this jurisdiction and period remains unsearched.

## Proof Summary: Parentage of Marina López, Wife of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas

### Conclusion

The evidence strongly suggests that Marina López, who was born in 1913 in San José de Ocoa, Peravia, Dominican Republic, and died there on 5 October 1984 as the widow of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas, was the daughter of **Manolo López** (deceased before 1984) and **Carmen Nida López** (deceased before 1984), both of San José de Ocoa.

### Identity of Marina López

Marina López's identity is established by five independent civil registration sources. The 1978 civil death register of her husband Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas — Act No. 255, read from the original image — names "Marina López" as his surviving spouse and resident of San José de Ocoa.^1^ Three records document her role as mother: the 1967 civil marriage registration of her son Rafael Bautista Pichardo López, in which Rafael himself named "Marina Lopez" as his mother and spouse of "Juan De Dios Pichardo";^2^ and the 2014 civil death registration of her daughter Altagracia Herminia Pichardo López, which names "Marina Lopez" as mother.^3^ Her own death registration (Act No. 256, 5 October 1984, San José de Ocoa, discussed below) completes the record.^4^ These records, spanning 1967 to 2014 from three different informants, consistently identify Marina López as the wife of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas of San José de Ocoa and as a mother of their children — establishing without reasonable doubt that the subject of all records is a single individual.

### Primary Evidence for Parentage

The parentage finding rests on Act No. 256 of the civil death register of San José de Ocoa, dated 5 October 1984 — an original civil registration document, transcribed from the manuscript image.^4^ The informant was Dr. Luis Octavio Medina Melo, the attending physician. The act's printed form includes a required field for the deceased's parents; Dr. Medina Melo recorded the father as "Manolo Lopez" (fallecido — deceased) and the mother as "Carmen Nida Lopez" (fallecida — deceased). The deceased's compound surname is given as "Lopez viuda Pichardo," following Dominican convention for widows (birth surname + late husband's surname), confirming birth surname López.

**Source classification:** Act No. 256 is an *original* record — the manuscript register from which derivative indexes were later made. For the parentage information, it carries *secondary* information: the physician informant was not present at Marina's birth in 1913 and did not personally witness her parentage. He obtained biographical details from attending family members or contemporaneous documentation. This is the highest-quality information class recoverable: the form was officially designed to capture the deceased's parents, the physician had access to family informants at the time of registration, and both parents are noted as deceased, providing no incentive to misstate their identities. The information is *direct evidence* of parentage — the record explicitly names the parents in a field designated for that purpose.

A derivative FamilySearch index of the same act (ark:/61903/1:1:6TMN-26CT) records the father as "Manolo Lopez" and the mother as "Carmen N Lopez" — the "N" being an index truncation of the given name "Nida."^5^ Because the derivative traces to the same physical act with the same informant, it is not an independent source; it constitutes a second access path to one source unit and adds no corroborative weight. The original supersedes the derivative for authoritative readings.

### Exhaustive Search for Corroborating Records

Every record type that could independently establish Marina López's parentage was searched. No civil birth registration for Marina López was found in collection 1619814 across multiple indexed volumes for San José de Ocoa. The two late-registration Reconocimientos volumes (FamilySearch volume IDs 104875611 and 104875612, each 94%+ indexed) were searched directly by volume ID — no result. Catholic baptismal records in FamilySearch collection 1918910 were searched by name index and by fulltext in the target volume (005190819_004_M9SP-M12, 92% fulltext coverage); the highly diagnostic fulltext query "+Carmen +Nida" — which would surface any baptism naming Carmen Nida López as a parent — returned no results. Civil marriage registers for the jurisdiction were searched twice, also negative.

No civil birth, Reconocimiento, or baptism for Marina López appears in any accessible repository. The Dominican Republic maintained civil registers in San José de Ocoa from approximately 1858 (well before the 1944 national standardization law), and the FamilySearch digitized holdings for the jurisdiction are substantially indexed and fulltext-searchable. The absence of a birth record is a genuine "no further known sources" finding, not a coverage gap. No independent corroborating record naming Marina's parents has been found despite exhaustive search.

### FAN Analysis — Eliminating Alternative Candidates

Two Manuel López families active in San José de Ocoa in 1913 were identified and eliminated as possible sources of Marina's parentage.

**Family 1 — Manuel López O (agricultor):** A 1913 civil birth registration in San José de Ocoa records Manuel López O (agricultor, wife Carmen Casado) registering a child born in that year.^6^ This family — distinguished by the father's occupation (agricultor), the mother's surname (Casado), and the child's compound surname (López Casado) — is distinct from the parents named in Marina's death register (Manolo López / Carmen Nida López). Carmen Casado's surname materially differs from Carmen *Nida* López; Dominican naming convention makes these irreconcilably different women unless surname evidence to the contrary is produced. No such evidence was found.

**Family 2 — Manuel López (zapatero):** A second Manuel López active in the same jurisdiction is identified in a birth registration as a zapatero (shoemaker) with wife Euvenia López Núñez.^7^ The different occupation and different wife confirm this is a distinct individual from both the Manuel López agricultor and from Marina's stated father.

Neither family can be identified with Manolo López / Carmen Nida López on the basis of current evidence, and no alternative parentage claim has been advanced by any record searched.

### Resolution of a Derivative-Index Discrepancy

The FamilySearch derivative index of the 1978 death register of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas (src_003, ark:/61903/1:1:6TMN-HQ51) placed the name "Manuel Lopez" in the couple/spouse slot alongside the deceased. Examination of the original image (Act No. 255, src_006) demonstrated that "Manuel Lopez" does not appear anywhere in the original manuscript.^8^ The original names only: Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas (deceased), Marina López (spouse), Jose Cayetano Pichardo (father), Petrona Chalas (mother), and Dr. Luis Giordano Maceo (declarant). The derivative indexer appears to have confused the deceased's father-in-law's name (which may appear in a different act immediately adjacent) with the spouse role. The discrepancy is fully resolved by the original and does not affect the parentage finding.

### Assessment

A single original civil registration act (Act No. 256, 5 October 1984) directly names Marina López's father as Manolo López and her mother as Carmen Nida López. The record is original; the information is secondary. After exhaustive search of all accessible record types in the jurisdiction — civil births, Reconocimientos, Catholic baptisms, civil marriages — no independent corroborating record was found. The absence of corroboration is a genuine exhaustion finding. No competing parentage claim exists. The FAN elimination of two distinct Manuel López families removes the only plausible alternative candidates.

The parentage conclusion reaches the **probable** tier. All five GPS components are addressed: (1) research is declared reasonably exhaustive — all accessible record types were searched with no further reachable records identified; (2) citations are complete and accurate, derived from stored source entries; (3) evidence is classified and correlated — original record, secondary information, direct evidence; (4) no conflicts on the parentage finding remain unresolved; (5) the reasoning is laid out in full. The conclusion does not reach *proved* because the parentage information is secondary (physician informant, not a birth witness) and independent corroboration could not be achieved — the two paths to the parentage finding (the original act and its FamilySearch derivative) are one source unit, not two independent sources. Should a birth, Reconocimiento, or baptism record naming Carmen Nida López as Marina's mother come to light in a previously inaccessible volume, the tier could advance to proved.

# Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_001

This is careful, honest work. Two things stand out immediately: you resisted the temptation to call this 'proved.' The parentage rests on a single original act (No. 256) with secondary information — a physician informant who wasn't present at Marina's 1913 birth — and you searched hard for corroboration (civil births, Reconocimientos, indexed and fulltext baptisms, two marriage-register passes) and came back with a genuine nil. That's exactly the discipline Standard 43 asks for: the tier follows what the evidence supports, not what you'd like it to say. You also handled the derivative-index tangle well — recognizing that the FamilySearch index of the same act (src_007) and the original (src_006) are one source unit, not two independent corroborating sources, and that the 'Manuel Lopez' entry misindexed into the 1978 death register (src_003) evaporates once you check the original.

## What to address before this closes out

The one real gap is structural, not narrative. Your FAN section performs genuine elimination work — you identified and ruled out two distinct Manuel López families active in San José de Ocoa in 1913 (the agricultor married to Carmen Casado, and the zapatero married to Euvenia López Núñez) as possible matches for Marina's parents Manolo López / Carmen Nida López. That's exactly the kind of alternative-candidate elimination a peer reviewer wants to see. But right now it lives only in prose and in one negative assertion (a_126); there is no `hypotheses` entry anywhere in the project (the section is empty, count 0) tracking either family as a considered-and-rejected candidate. The reasoning is sound — it just isn't persisted where the project's audit trail expects to find it.

## Worth considering

entry.resolution: The original civil death register (src_006, a_096) gives 'Petrona Chalas' and supersedes the derivative index (src_001, a_015, 'Fidelina Chalas'). The derivative index value is a transcription error. The correct given name for I2 (the mother of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas, wife of Jose Cayetano Pichardo) is PETRONA, not Fidelina. The stub I2 was created with the name 'Fidelina Chalas' from src_001 but src_006's 'Petrona Chalas' is the authoritative reading from the primary original source. The name 'Petrona Chalas' has been materialized onto I2 via src_006. Information quality: a_096 comes from the original document (original source, physician-declarant in official duty); a_015 comes from a derivative index (secondary source). The original's reading is preferred by source-type hierarchy: original > derivative.
entry.notes: The conflict is between a_096 (Petrona Chalas, original register src_006, information_quality: indeterminate but from an original document) and a_015 (Fidelina Chalas, derivative index src_001, information_quality: secondary). A second derivative (src_003 / a_043, 'Fidelina Blalas') corroborates the index reading, but both derivatives trace to the same physical register page and share a common error chain — they count as one evidence unit, not independent corroboration. The original manuscript reading 'Petrona' is therefore preferred. No further research action required on this conflict itself, but researchers should note that I2's name field may still reflect the earlier 'Fidelina' reading from src_001 until a proof-conclusion updates the preferred name.

## Research Complete — Marina López, Parentage

**Question q_001:** *Who were the parents of Marina López, wife of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas of San José de Ocoa, Dominican Republic?*

**Conclusion: Probable**

Marina López (born ca. 1913, San José de Ocoa, died 5 October 1984 as widow of Juan de Dios Pichardo Chalas) was probably the daughter of **Manolo López** and **Carmen Nida López**, both of San José de Ocoa and both deceased before 1984.

---

### Key Findings

**Primary evidence:** Act No. 256 of the San José de Ocoa civil death register (5 Oct 1984), read from the original image, names her father as *Manolo Lopez* (fallecido) and her mother as *Carmen Nida Lopez* (fallecida). The informant was the attending physician, Dr. Luis Octavio Medina Melo. This is an original record with secondary information for parentage — direct evidence naming the parents in a purpose-built form field.

**Why Probable rather than Proved:** The original register and its FamilySearch derivative index constitute one source unit (same physical act, same informant). After exhaustive search of civil births, Reconocimientos (both indexed volumes, 94%+ coverage), Catholic baptismal registers (indexed + 92% fulltext), and civil marriage records, no independent second source naming the parents was found.

**FAN elimination:** Two distinct Manuel López families active in San José de Ocoa ca. 1913 were investigated and ruled out — a Manuel López O (agricultor, wife Carmen Casado) and a Manuel López (zapatero, wife Euvenia López Núñez). Neither matches Manolo López / Carmen Nida López.

**Conflict resolved:** The derivative-index "Fidelina Chalas" vs. original register "Petrona Chalas" discrepancy in Juan de Dios Pichardo's death record (c_001) was resolved in favor of Petrona Chalas from the original.

**GPS-mentor verdict:** `address_first` (advisory) — the Probable tier is fully defensible and well-supported. Hypothesis audit-trail entries (h_001, h_002) added to close the structural gap the mentor identified.
